items.title: Sales After Ads
items.question: A shop raised sales right after running an ad, so the owner credits the ad. Which assumption is doing the work?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Crediting the ad quietly rules out every other possible explanation for the rise.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is no other cause. Season, price, and weather could all explain the change, so the argument assumes them away.
items.lessonContent:
Sequence alone never proves a cause.
Every causal claim rules out rivals.
Name the alternatives before concluding.
Test the claim with a comparison.
Share this: list one rival explanation for a change you noticed.

items.title: Tomorrows Market
items.question: A trader expects tomorrow's market to repeat today's pattern. What is being assumed?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The expectation rests on the idea that what happened before will happen again.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is past predicts future. That link holds only when the underlying conditions stay similar.
items.lessonContent:
Patterns persist only while their causes persist.
History is a guide, not a guarantee.
Ask what would break the pattern.
Update when conditions change.
Share this: name one condition that could break a trend you rely on.

items.title: One Neighbourhood Poll
items.question: A poll of one neighbourhood is used to predict a national election. What must be assumed?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Projecting from one area requires that it mirrors the wider population.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a representative sample. If the district differs in any relevant way, its result will not travel.
items.lessonContent:
Wider claims need samples that mirror the whole.
Ask who was left out.
Small unrepresentative groups mislead badly.
Compare the sample with the target.
Share this: check who a poll or survey never reached.

items.title: Moving Together
items.question: Two variables move together, so a writer declares one causes the other. Which assumption is hidden?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The argument treats mere co-movement as proof of a causal link.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is correlation implies causation. A third factor or pure coincidence can produce the same pattern.
items.lessonContent:
Co-movement is not causation.
Hidden factors can drive both variables.
Look for a mechanism before concluding.
Use comparisons to test the link.
Share this: find one correlation today and name a possible hidden factor.

items.title: Friendly Offer
items.question: A negotiator treats a rival's helpful offer at face value. What is being assumed?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Taking the offer at face value assumes the other side means exactly what it says.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is honest motives. Offers can carry hidden conditions, and assuming goodwill can be costly.
items.lessonContent:
Stated intentions are not guaranteed intentions.
Ask what the other side gains.
Check for hidden terms.
Trust is a conclusion, not a default.
Share this: ask what the other party gains from one offer you receive.

items.title: Five Year Budget
items.question: A five-year plan totals future costs without adjusting for rising prices. What is being assumed?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Adding raw figures across years assumes the value of money stays put.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is stable prices. In reality costs drift, so a plan must adjust each year's figures.
items.lessonContent:
Money changes value over time.
Compare figures only at a common baseline.
Long plans need an inflation assumption.
State every assumption in a projection.
Share this: adjust one long-range figure for rising prices.

items.title: Perfect Calculators
items.question: An economic model predicts behaviour as if everyone calculates perfectly. What is being assumed?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The model assumes people weigh every option with perfect consistency.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is rational actors. Real people use habits, emotions, and shortcuts that models may miss.
items.lessonContent:
Models embed assumptions about people.
Real behaviour includes emotion and habit.
Stress-test a model at its edges.
Compare predictions with observed behaviour.
Share this: watch for one choice today made by habit rather than calculation.

items.title: One Shared Word
items.question: A debate proceeds as if a key word means the same to both sides. What is being assumed?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The exchange assumes the contested term is being used identically by everyone.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a fixed definition. Disputes often hide behind words each side defines differently.
items.lessonContent:
Ambiguous terms create fake agreement and fake conflict.
Define key words before arguing.
Check whether both sides mean the same thing.
Rephrase to surface the gap.
Share this: define one word you use loosely in your next discussion.

items.title: Specialist Consensus
items.question: A claim is accepted because specialists in the field repeat it. What is being assumed?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The argument leans on the idea that a shared view among specialists settles the matter.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is expert agreement. Consensus can be genuine or an echo, so the reasoning behind it still matters.
items.lessonContent:
Appeals to authority need the reasoning too.
Distinguish agreement from independent evidence.
Ask what the experts based the view on.
Check whether all voices agree.
Share this: ask for the reason behind one expert opinion you accept.

items.title: Last Years Rule
items.question: A rule from last year is applied to a case this year without checking for amendments. What is being assumed?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Applying the old rule assumes nothing relevant has changed since.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is unchanged rules. Rules and circumstances shift, and stale guidance can mislead.
items.lessonContent:
Past rules can expire or change.
Verify currency before applying.
Ask when the rule was last updated.
Stale information quietly misleads.
Share this: check the date on one rule or policy you rely on.

items.title: Unchecked Figures
items.question: A conclusion rests on statistics that were never verified. What is being assumed?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The argument takes the input numbers as correct without checking them.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is accurate data. Errors early on propagate through every conclusion drawn from them.
items.lessonContent:
Conclusions inherit the quality of their inputs.
Verify figures before using them.
Check the source and the method.
Trace errors back to their origin.
Share this: verify one number you repeat without checking.

items.title: Confident Voice
items.question: A report is trusted because its author sounds sure. What is being assumed?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Confidence is taken as a sign that the source is fair and informed.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is an unbiased source. Assurance and accuracy are different things, and bias can sound certain.
items.lessonContent:
Delivery style is not evidence.
Confidence can mask bias or error.
Check the source's interests.
Separate tone from substance.
Share this: separate confidence from evidence in one claim you hear today.

items.title: Twenty Year Line
items.question: A rising graph is extended twenty years into the future. What is being assumed?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Extending the line assumes the same rate keeps going indefinitely.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a lasting trend. Limits, saturation, and reversals can bend the line sharply.
items.lessonContent:
Trends encounter limits over time.
Extrapolation assumes conditions persist.
Ask what could slow or reverse growth.
Use ranges instead of a single line.
Share this: question one forecast that extends a trend far ahead.

items.title: Lab to Factory
items.question: A result from a clean laboratory is applied to a messy factory floor. What is being assumed?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Transferring the result assumes the surroundings have no effect on it.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is static conditions. Different environments introduce variables that the original test excluded.
items.lessonContent:
Results depend on the setting that produced them.
Transfer needs matching conditions.
Ask what the first test controlled for.
Expect real-world variance.
Share this: name one condition a controlled test leaves out.

items.title: Order as Cause
items.question: Two events happen in order, so the first is blamed for the second. What is being assumed?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The reasoning assumes that coming first means causing what follows.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is sequence as cause. Many things happen in order without any causal link.
items.lessonContent:
Order alone does not create a cause.
Coincidence can imitate causation.
Look for a mechanism between events.
Test by changing the order.
Share this: find one pair of events that merely happened in order.

items.title: Polite Question
items.question: A question is answered literally because it was asked politely. What is being assumed?
items.correctExplanation: Right. A courteous tone is taken as proof that the asker wants a straight answer.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is genuine curiosity. Questions can be rhetorical, testing, or hostile while sounding mild.
items.lessonContent:
Tone can disguise intent.
Ask why a question is being asked.
Consider the asker's incentives.
Answer the purpose, not just the words.
Share this: consider the motive behind one question you are asked today.

items.title: This or That
items.question: A choice is framed as one thing or another with no room for a third path. What is being assumed?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The framing assumes the two presented paths exhaust every possibility.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is only two options. Real situations often include alternatives that the framing hides.
items.lessonContent:
Framings can shrink the option space.
Ask whether a third path exists.
Refuse binary boxes before deciding.
Generate options before choosing.
Share this: invent one extra option for a choice you face today.

items.title: Lone Counterexample
items.question: A single counterexample is dismissed as a fluke to protect a general claim. What is being assumed?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The move assumes the contrary case carries no information about the rule.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is an irrelevant exception. Sometimes one real case is enough to show a claim is overstated.
items.lessonContent:
Exceptions can be the most informative cases.
Ask why one case does not fit.
Weak rules rely on excusing outliers.
Revise a claim to accommodate evidence.
Share this: examine one exception you usually dismiss.

items.title: Eyewitness Account
items.question: An eyewitness account is treated as settling a disputed event. What is being assumed?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The account is taken as accurate without checking the witness's vantage or memory.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a reliable witness. Attention, bias, and time can all distort what someone reports.
items.lessonContent:
Memory is reconstructive, not photographic.
Check vantage and conditions.
Corroborate accounts independently.
Weigh confidence against accuracy.
Share this: ask how well placed one witness really was.

items.title: Share Price Truth
items.question: A share price is treated as the true value of a company. What is being assumed?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The reasoning assumes prices already reflect all relevant information.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is efficient markets. Prices can overshoot or lag, driven by sentiment as well as value.
items.lessonContent:
Prices mix information with sentiment.
Markets can be wrong for long stretches.
Separate value from current quotation.
Look for the reasoning behind a price.
Share this: question one price as if it were a settled truth.

items.title: One Success Story
items.question: One successful case is used to prescribe a method for everyone. What is being assumed?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The argument assumes that what worked once will work broadly.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a general rule. A single success ignores failures and the conditions that made it possible.
items.lessonContent:
One case cannot establish a rule.
Ask how many tried and failed.
Conditions matter as much as method.
Demand more than a story.
Share this: ask how many failures a success story leaves out.

items.title: Average Resident
items.question: An average income is used to describe how a typical resident lives. What is being assumed?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The description assumes the average reflects a normal individual experience.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a typical average. Skewed distributions make the average describe almost no one.
items.lessonContent:
Averages can hide extreme values.
Ask about the spread, not just the middle.
Few people may resemble the average.
Use median or ranges when skew is high.
Share this: check whether one average actually describes anyone you know.

items.title: Single Big Factor
items.question: A complex outcome is attributed to one clear factor. What is being assumed?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The explanation assumes one factor is enough to account for everything observed.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a single cause. Most outcomes emerge from several interacting factors.
items.lessonContent:
Complex results usually have many inputs.
Single-cause stories feel satisfying but mislead.
List contributing factors before concluding.
Weigh their relative influence.
Share this: list three causes for one outcome you usually simplify.

items.title: Symptom After Remedy
items.question: Because a symptom eased after a remedy was taken, the remedy is credited with the cure. What is being assumed?
acceptedAnswers: It worked because it came first
items.correctExplanation: Right. The reasoning assumes the timing alone establishes that the remedy did the work.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is causal timing. Recovery may have happened anyway, through natural course or expectation.
items.lessonContent:
Improvement can occur without intervention.
Compare with a control to isolate effects.
Beware the natural course of symptoms.
Timing is necessary but not sufficient.
Share this: ask what would have happened with no treatment at all.

items.title: Unquestioned Premise
items.question: An argument proceeds without ever questioning whether its starting claim is true. What is being assumed?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Valid reasoning from a false start still yields a false conclusion.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a true premise. Soundness requires both good form and true starting claims.
items.lessonContent:
Validity and truth are different checks.
A flawless argument can rest on a false start.
Examine each premise for support.
Test the conclusion against reality.
Share this: question the first premise of one argument you accept.
